predicted_disagreements: Shannon vs Grothendieck, axis source-corpus + methodology: Shannon can over-read AI model-use promise from research prose; Grothendieck exposes that by separating Lean theorem, formal witness, prose bridge, and ML experiment. Shannon exposes Grothendieck's proof-purity bias by identifying commercially meaningful model-evaluation methods that are not theorem claims.

Shannon vs Curie, axis source-corpus + methodology: Shannon centers known model-use lanes and can miss hidden siblings; Curie exposes that by doing an inventory-style sweep over the full Lean formalization tree. Shannon exposes Curie's search-term bias by preserving semantic lanes that do not contain the obvious words.

Grothendieck vs Curie, axis source-corpus + temporal-prior: Grothendieck can over-center current theorem surfaces; Curie exposes that by surfacing older, adjacent, or sidecar research artifacts. Grothendieck exposes Curie's artifact-counting bias by marking which hits actually bear a formal or definitional load.

predicted_disagreements: Lakatos vs Taleb, axis attack-vector: Lakatos can over-demote because a component has precedent; Taleb exposes that by preserving witnessed combinations with concrete falsifiable tests. Lakatos exposes Taleb's witness-only bias by narrowing claims already owned by external programs.

Lakatos vs Quine, axis attack-vector: Lakatos can import broad market or research labels; Quine exposes that by forcing each term to preserve meaning across AI, Lean, and BP contexts. Lakatos exposes Quine's local-definition bias by testing whether definitions survive external reading.

Taleb vs Quine, axis attack-vector: Taleb can reduce claims to artifact counts; Quine exposes that by checking whether the artifact proves the defined claim. Taleb exposes Quine's wording-only bias by requiring a witness or next experiment for each refined definition.
